skill.name: Infer the why: work out a reason the text never states
skill.why: Texts don't explain everything. Good readers fill the gaps with clues.
skill.how: Ask why it happened. Find the clues, add what you know, and check it fits.

steps.say: Texts show you what happened, but not always why. Why did Mo open every window?

show.nudge: That's what happened. Find a clue to why it happened.

show.text: The kitchen was full of smoke.

show.nudge: A sleeping cat doesn't explain open windows. Try another.

steps.ask: Tap the clue that helps explain why.
steps.win: Yes! Smoke is the clue. Now I add what I know about smoke.

steps.say: I know smoke stings your eyes. Open windows let it out.

show.text: The kitchen was full of smoke.

steps.ask: So why did Mo open every window?

options.text: to let the smoke out
to let the cat out
options.reason: The cat was asleep. Look at the clue about the kitchen.

options.text: to wave to his friends
options.reason: No clue in the text is about friends. Look at the clue about the kitchen.

steps.win: Yes! The text never says why. I worked it out from a clue. That's an inference.

steps.say: Now I check. Does another clue in the text fit my reason?

show.nudge: That's my reason. Find a clue in the text that fits it.
Red socks don't make smoke. Find a clue about the smoke.

show.text: The toast was black and smoking.

show.nudge: Tuesday doesn't explain smoke. Find a clue about the smoke.

steps.ask: Tap the clue that fits my reason.
steps.win: Yes! Burnt toast explains the smoke. My reason fits.

steps.say: Zed has another idea: Mo was just hot. Here's the start of the story.

show.text: It was a freezing winter morning.

show.nudge: That's what Mo did. Which clue shows he wasn't hot?

show.text: The kitchen was full of smoke.
show.nudge: Smoke is the real reason. Which clue shows Mo wasn't hot?

steps.ask: Tap the clue that shows Zed's idea is wrong.
steps.win: Yes! Nobody is hot on a freezing morning. A reason from your head must fit ALL the clues.

steps.say: One more. Pick the reason that every clue backs up.

show.text: Pickle hid under the bed and shook.
When the storm stopped, he came out.

options.text: He was scared of the thunder.
He was in trouble for chewing a shoe.
options.reason: Dogs do hide when they're in trouble. But does any clue say he chewed something?

options.text: He was playing hide and seek.
options.reason: Playing dogs wag and bounce. Pickle shook. Look at when he came out.

steps.win: Yes! Thunder boomed, and he came out when it stopped. Every clue fits.

terms.means: Words in the text that point to the reason.
The why you work out. The text never says it.
Another clue. Your reason must fit every clue, not just one.

examples.text: The kitchen was full of smoke.
Pickle came out when it stopped.
He was scared of the thunder.

card.test: Ask why. Find the clue, add what you know, then check it fits ALL the clues.

creature.name: Cubbler
creature.blurb: A wombat that leaves neat cube-shaped clues wherever it goes. It never tells you why it dug, so you'll have to work it out.

write.ask: Write the next sentence. Give a clue that shows why Gus held his nose, but don't say why.
given: Gus opened the fridge, held his nose and backed away.
checks: I didn't use 'because' or say the reason.
My clue is something you could see, hear or smell.
A reader could work out the why from my clue.

encounters.frame: A Cubbler is snuffling around the classroom door. Something odd is going on.
encounters.text: Mo walked into class wearing a big woolly beanie. It was the hottest day of the year. Everyone else was in shorts and thongs. The teacher asked him to take it off. 'No thanks,' said Mo, and pulled it down even lower. He kept it on all morning, even when sweat dripped off his nose. At lunch, a gust of wind blew it off. Under it, his hair was bright green. 'The box said brown,' he groaned.
encounters.prompt: Why did Mo keep his beanie on?
encounters.success: His hair was bright green under it. The text never says 'to hide it', but the clues do.

options.text: because he was cold
options.reason: It was the hottest day of the year, and sweat was dripping off his nose.

options.text: to hide his green hair
because the teacher told him to
options.reason: The teacher asked him to take it off, not keep it on.

encounters.frame: Tully is telling the crew about the best part of Saturday's footy.
encounters.text: Halfway through the footy game, the umpire blew her whistle. Everyone stopped. A big brown dog was racing across the oval. The footy was in its mouth. Three players chased after it. The dog thought this was a great game. It ran in circles and wagged its tail. It took ten minutes to get the ball back. The ball was very soggy. Tully said it was the best part of the game.
encounters.prompt: Why did three players chase the dog?
encounters.success: The footy was in the dog's mouth. You can't play without the ball, so they chased it.

options.text: to get the footy back
to give the friendly dog a pat
options.reason: The dog had their footy in its mouth. They wanted the ball, not a pat.

options.text: because it bit someone
options.reason: Nothing in the text says anyone was bitten. The dog was playing.

encounters.frame: The crew camped on a hill to watch shooting stars. The Cubbler dug itself a warm burrow.
encounters.text: The crew camped out on the hill to watch the meteor shower. It was a clear night, so the stars were bright. It was also freezing. There was frost on the grass. And the mozzies were everywhere. Zed put on two beanies. Indi zipped her jacket up to her chin. Tully put bug spray on her arms. Mo wrapped himself in three blankets. Gus kept slapping his neck. At midnight, a shooting star zipped across the sky. Everyone cheered.
encounters.prompt: Match each thing the crew did to the reason they did it.
encounters.success: Beanies, jackets and blankets are for the cold. Bug spray and slapping are for the mozzies.

items.text: Zed put on two beanies.
items.reason: Beanies keep your head warm, and there was frost on the grass.

items.text: Indi zipped her jacket up to her chin.
items.reason: A jacket zipped up high keeps you warm, and there was frost on the grass.

items.text: Tully put bug spray on her arms.
items.reason: Bug spray keeps mozzies away.

items.text: Mo wrapped himself in three blankets.
items.reason: Blankets keep you warm on a freezing night.

items.text: Gus kept slapping his neck.
items.reason: People slap at their skin when mozzies land on them.

encounters.frame: Zed has homework. His little brother has drums.
encounters.text: Zed was trying to do his maths homework. Next door, his little brother was learning the drums. Boom. Crash. Boom-boom-CRASH. He had been playing the same song for two hours. He still couldn't get it right. Zed's pencil jumped every time the cymbal crashed. At last, Zed put on his big headphones. He didn't play any music. He just sat there in the quiet and finished his maths.
encounters.prompt: Why did Zed put on his headphones?
encounters.success: The drumming was so loud his pencil jumped. Headphones with no music just block out noise.

options.reason: The text says he didn't play any music.

options.reason: Nothing in the text is about cold. Look at the noise next door.

encounters.frame: Wren had a surprise visitor in the backyard. The Cubbler was very jealous.
encounters.text: It was 43 degrees in Hollowgum on Saturday, the hottest day in ten years. At about two o'clock, Wren heard scratching on the back fence. A koala had climbed down from the gum tree and walked across the lawn to the swimming pool. It sat on the top step and drank and drank. It didn't swim. It didn't even get its bottom wet. Wren's dog, Pickle, was asleep inside under the fan, so nothing had chased it. The creek at the bottom of the hill had dried up two weeks ago. After about ten minutes, the koala climbed slowly back up the tree. Wren left a big bowl of water at the bottom of the trunk, just in case. The next morning, the bowl was empty.
encounters.prompt: Why did the koala come down to the pool?
encounters.success: It was 43 degrees and the creek had dried up. It drank and drank, so it came for water.

options.text: A dog chased it out of the tree.
options.reason: Pickle was asleep inside, so nothing chased it.

options.text: It wanted a swim to cool off.
options.reason: It didn't swim. It didn't even get its bottom wet.

options.text: It needed a drink.

encounters.frame: The Cubbler is digging in the sand at Hollowgum Beach. It has found something blue.
encounters.text: Hollowgum Beach was packed on Sunday morning. The sky was clear, the sea was calm, and the water was the warmest it had been all summer. Then, at about eleven o'clock, people started running out of the water. 'Ow! Something stung me!' yelled a boy, holding his arm. Along the edge of the sand, hundreds of little blue blobs had washed up. They looked like tiny balloons with long, stringy tails. A few minutes later, the lifesavers put up red flags and blew their whistles. Nobody was allowed back in the water for the rest of the day. The lifesavers spent the afternoon looking after stung swimmers and scooping the blue blobs into buckets.
encounters.prompt: Why did the lifesavers close the beach?
encounters.success: People were being stung, and stingy blue blobs had washed up. Swimming wasn't safe.

options.text: Stinging blue creatures had washed in.
A big storm was coming in from the sea.
options.reason: The sky was clear and the sea was calm. There's no sign of a storm.

options.text: The water was too cold.
options.reason: The text says the water was the warmest it had been all summer.

encounters.frame: Gus's robot butler is acting strangely. The Cubbler is hiding under the table.
encounters.text: Gus's robot butler, Jeeves, had been working perfectly all week. On Friday afternoon, though, things got weird. At lunch, Mo had been fiddling with the buttons on Jeeves's control panel, giggling to himself. He had pressed one marked PARTY MODE. At three o'clock, a little red battery light on Jeeves's back started flashing. Gus didn't notice, because he was busy in the lab. By four o'clock, Jeeves was rolling around the kitchen blasting loud music. Rainbow lights were flashing on his head. He was also moving slower and slower, and his arms had drooped until they hung limp by his sides. At five o'clock, he stopped in the middle of the floor. He didn't move again until Gus plugged him in.
encounters.prompt: Match each strange thing Jeeves did to the reason for it.
encounters.success: Music and rainbow lights came from party mode. Slowing down, drooping and stopping came from the flat battery.

bins: because his battery was running low

items.text: Jeeves blasted loud music.
items.reason: Loud music is what you'd expect from a button called PARTY MODE.

items.text: Rainbow lights flashed on his head.
items.reason: Flashing rainbow lights are a party thing, and Mo pressed PARTY MODE.

items.text: Jeeves moved slower and slower.
items.reason: Machines slow down when their batteries run low, and his battery light was flashing.

items.text: His arms drooped until they hung limp.
items.reason: Limp arms mean he was running out of power. Party mode made him louder and brighter, not floppier.

items.text: He stopped in the middle of the floor.
items.reason: Plugging him in got him going again, so a flat battery stopped him.

encounters.frame: Zed wrote a note about the 'haunted' hall. One part is wrong.
encounters.text: For three weeks, people in Hollowgum had been whispering about the old church hall. Every Thursday night, its lights came on at seven o'clock. Strange, high voices floated out of the windows. 'It's haunted,' said Zed. On the fourth Thursday, the crew crept up to the hall to look. Through the window, they saw twenty old people standing in a circle. Each one was holding a sheet of music. A woman at the piano tapped a stick and called out, 'From the top, everyone!' The voices started again. A man in the front row sang so high that a glass of water on the piano wobbled. At eight o'clock, everyone came out holding cups of tea and arguing about biscuits.

encounters.frame: Mum has a plan. The Cubbler can smell chocolate in the freezer.
encounters.text: Mum bought a big packet of choc-chip biscuits for the school fete on Saturday. The last time she bought biscuits, the whole packet vanished in one night. Mo had crumbs on his pillow the next morning, and a chocolate smudge on his ear. This time, Mum tipped the frozen peas into a bowl. She put the biscuits inside the empty peas box and pushed it right to the back of the freezer. On Friday night, Mo opened the freezer and looked around. He moved the ice cream. He looked at the peas box, then shut the door. Mo hates peas. 'Where are the biscuits?' he asked. 'What biscuits?' said Mum, smiling.
encounters.prompt: Why did Mum put the biscuits in the peas box?
encounters.success: Mo ate the last packet, and he hates peas. A peas box is the last place he'd look.

options.text: So Mo wouldn't find them.
Because Mo asked her to keep them cold.
options.reason: Mo didn't even know where they were. He asks, 'Where are the biscuits?'

encounters.frame: The school band has a problem. The Cubbler has been listening at the music room door.
encounters.text: Sam had been practising his trumpet solo for 'Sunrise March' every night for six weeks. The concert was only two weeks away. His neighbours knew every note. He even played it in the shower, which was difficult. On Monday, he came to school with a brand-new set of braces, shiny and silver across his top and bottom teeth. At band practice that afternoon, he lifted his trumpet, blew one note and winced. He tried again, and his eyes watered. He put the trumpet down on his knee and pressed his lips together. At lunch the next day, he ate only mashed potato, very slowly. After practice, he went to see Mr Okoro, the band teacher. On Tuesday, Mr Okoro announced that Lucy would play the solo at the concert instead. Lucy's mouth fell open, because she hadn't even known the solo was free. Lucy played the solo beautifully. Sam played the triangle. He hit it perfectly, every time, and smiled carefully with his mouth closed.
encounters.prompt: Why did Sam stop playing the trumpet solo?
encounters.success: The pain started the day he got braces. Soft food and a closed-mouth smile point to his teeth.

options.text: His lips were sore from six weeks of practice.
options.reason: He practised for six weeks with no trouble. The pain started the day his braces went on.

options.text: Lucy asked to have the solo.
options.reason: Lucy didn't even know the solo was free. Her mouth fell open.

options.text: His new braces made playing hurt.
He was too nervous to play a solo at the concert.
options.reason: Nothing shows nerves. He winces in pain, and he eats only soft mashed potato.

encounters.frame: There are worms all over the back veranda. The Cubbler is very interested.
encounters.text: Gus keeps a worm farm on the back veranda: three stacked trays full of soil, food scraps and about two thousand worms. On Tuesday, he fed them a whole pumpkin, which they love. On Wednesday night, a huge storm rolled across Hollowgum. It rained so hard that the gutters overflowed, and water poured off the veranda roof for hours, right on top of the worm farm. On Thursday morning, Gus opened the back door and nearly stepped on a worm. Then another. Then about forty more, all wriggling across the tiles away from the farm. Gus checked the lid, and it was still clipped on tight. The worms had squeezed out through the little drain holes in the bottom. When he lifted the top tray, the bottom tray was full to the brim with brown water, like a tiny swimming pool. Gus spent the whole morning picking up worms with a spoon and putting them in a bucket of dry soil. Mo helped by screaming.
encounters.prompt: Why did the worms crawl out of the farm?
encounters.success: Water poured onto the farm all night and the bottom tray was full. The worms were escaping the flood.

options.text: They were hungry and looking for more food.
options.reason: Gus fed them a whole pumpkin on Tuesday, which they love.

options.text: The lid had been left off.
options.reason: The lid was still clipped on tight. They squeezed out through the drain holes.

options.text: The loud storm frightened them out.
options.reason: The storm matters, but look in the bottom tray. What did all that rain leave behind?

options.text: Their farm had filled with water.

encounters.frame: Tully wants to know why the coach made the call she did. So does the Cubbler.
encounters.text: With four seconds left in the netball grand final, the scores were level, and Hollowgum had one last shot. Coach Dee called a time-out and looked along her team. Ruby, her own daughter, was the tallest player on court, but she had missed her last three shots and was staring at the ground. Jess had scored the most goals all season, but she had twisted her ankle in the second quarter and was sitting on the bench with an ice pack. Then there was Mia. Mia hadn't missed a single shot all afternoon. Before the game, while the others were bouncing around nervously, she had been sitting on the bench calmly reading a book. Coach Dee handed her the ball and said, 'Your shot.' Mia stepped up, breathed out, and the ball dropped through the ring without touching the sides. Ruby ran over and lifted her right off the ground.

encounters.frame: It's the school art show. Indi's painting is hiding under a sheet.
encounters.text: Indi's painting had been finished for a week. It was the biggest thing she had ever painted: her nan, sitting in her garden among her prize-winning tomatoes, with her old dog, Biscuit, asleep at her feet. The paint had dried days ago. The art show opened in the school hall at six o'clock, and Indi's painting was hung right by the door. But Indi had draped a bedsheet over it and stuck on a sign that said DO NOT PEEK. Zed peeked anyway, and Indi chased him out of the hall. All evening, she kept checking her watch and looking out at the car park. Nan's bus from Pine Gully was due at seven. At five past seven, Nan walked through the door. Indi grabbed her hand, led her to the painting and pulled off the sheet. Nan stood there for a long time without saying anything. Then she said, 'You've even got Biscuit's snore right.'
encounters.prompt: Why did Indi keep her painting covered until seven o'clock?
encounters.success: She waited for Nan's bus, then uncovered it the moment Nan arrived. It was a surprise for Nan.

options.text: She wanted to surprise Nan with it.
The paint was still wet.
options.reason: The text says the paint had dried days ago.

options.text: She was embarrassed by how it looked.
options.reason: She hung it right by the door. And look who she kept watching for all evening.

options.text: She wanted to wait until the hall was full.
options.reason: She pulled off the sheet the moment Nan walked in, not when a crowd arrived.

encounters.frame: Maxx Vantablack is streaming a 'rescue'. Wren has been watching the replay with the Cubbler.
encounters.text: MAXX VANTABLACK LIVE: RESCUE DAY! Maxx has millions of followers, and most of them believe he rescues creatures for a living. 'Vantafam, welcome back! Today I'm saving a super-rare Glimmerwing from the dangerous wild. Look how happy it is in its new home!' He swung the camera towards a small glass box on his desk. Inside, a little silver creature was flapping against the walls, again and again, until its wings made a soft tapping sound on the glass. 'Ha, it's dancing!' said Maxx. The chat filled with hearts. Then one message popped up in red: 'Is it trying to get out?' Another followed: 'Why does it keep hitting the glass?' Maxx stopped smiling. He leaned forward, read the messages, and quickly tilted the camera up towards the ceiling, so that the box disappeared from the shot. 'Oops, camera slipped!' he said brightly. 'Anyway, let's talk about my new hoodie range.' He held up a hoodie with his own face on it. For the rest of the stream, the camera never pointed at the desk again, even though his battery showed 96 per cent and the room was perfectly well lit. Afterwards, Wren watched the replay four times, pausing each time on the moment the camera tilted. Then she quietly started packing her rescue kit.

encounters.success: With a full battery and good light, the only reason left is hiding the creature's struggle.

encounters.prompt: Tap the clue that explains why Captain Loretta turned back early.
encounters.success: The radio warned of ninety-kilometre winds by afternoon. She turned back to beat the storm home.

parts: Log of the fishing boat Saltbush, Thursday. We left Hollowgum harbour at five o'clock this morning under a clear, pink sky, planning to fish the deep reef until sunset. The forecast the night before had promised light winds all day, and Loretta has fished these waters for thirty years.

parts.tap: By nine o'clock our nets were already half full of snapper, the best catch we'd had all month.
parts.reason: A great catch would make you want to stay out. It doesn't explain turning back.

parts.tap: Young Kip was seasick twice over the side, but he felt better after a ginger biscuit.
parts.reason: Kip felt better after his biscuit, so he isn't the reason they went home.

parts: At half past nine, the radio crackled.

parts.tap: The weather bureau announced that a fierce southerly change would hit the coast by early afternoon, with winds of up to ninety kilometres an hour.

parts: Captain Loretta listened carefully, then looked south, where a thin grey line had appeared along the horizon. She said nothing, but she pulled in the nets, turned the Saltbush around and pushed the engine as hard as it would go.

parts.tap: On the way back, a pod of dolphins rode our bow wave for almost a kilometre.
parts.reason: The dolphins came after she had already turned around.

parts: We tied up at the jetty at twenty past twelve. By one o'clock, the harbour was white with foam, and the masts of the moored boats were swinging like windscreen wipers. Captain Loretta poured herself a cup of tea and said, 'Snapper keeps.'

encounters.frame: The museum's cleaning robots have gone strange. The Cubbler has been reading the guard's report.
encounters.text: Hollowgum Museum has a team of twelve cleaning robots, six in the east wing and six in the west wing. They are round, about the size of a cake tin, and each one has a name painted on its lid. For two years, they have swept the floors every night without any trouble. This week, however, the night guard, Ron, wrote a report full of surprises in neat capital letters. On Tuesday evening, every robot in the building downloaded a software update. On Wednesday morning, the cleaners polished the floors of the east wing with a new, extra-shiny wax, but they ran out before they could do the west wing. That night, all twelve robots began announcing the time in French every fifteen minutes. All twelve also started humming the same tune, which nobody could name. Meanwhile, the six robots in the east wing kept skidding sideways, spinning in slow circles and bumping into display cases. One of them slid gently into the dinosaur skeleton and stayed there until morning, pressed against its leg. The west-wing robots, by contrast, cleaned in perfectly straight lines between their announcements. The museum has now undone the update and covered the east-wing floors with rubber mats, and the dinosaur is reported to be unharmed.
encounters.prompt: Match each strange thing the robots did to its most likely cause.
encounters.success: What all twelve did came from the update. What only the east-wing robots did came from the wax.

items.text: Robots announced the time in French.
items.reason: All twelve did this, in both wings. Only the update reached every robot.

items.text: Robots hummed a tune nobody could name.
items.reason: All twelve hummed, including the west wing, which had no wax.

items.text: Robots skidded sideways.
items.reason: Only east-wing robots skidded, and only the east wing got the shiny wax.

items.text: Robots spun in slow circles.
items.reason: Only east-wing robots spun. The west-wing robots, on unwaxed floors, went straight.

items.text: A robot slid into the dinosaur skeleton.
items.reason: Sliding is what happens on a slippery floor, and the west wing had no new wax.

encounters.frame: The Hollowgum Herald is puzzled by the bakery. The Cubbler can smell fresh bread.
encounters.text: Every morning for twenty-two years, Rosa Bellini has baked bread at the Hollowgum Bakery, and every afternoon she has sold it at full price. Her sourdough is famous across the island, and on Saturdays the queue stretches past the chemist. So people were surprised on Thursday when they found a hand-written sign in the window: FREE BREAD TODAY. TAKE AS MUCH AS YOU LIKE. One man took eleven loaves and a bag of rolls. By lunchtime, the shelves were bare. Some customers were suspicious and asked whether the bread was stale, but it was still warm, and the smell drifted all the way down the street. Others wondered if it was Rosa's birthday, but her birthday is in June, and this is November. On Friday morning, the bakery stayed dark. Another sign had appeared, taped neatly beneath the first: CLOSED FOR TWO WEEKS WHILE WE PUT IN A NEW OVEN. SEE YOU SOON. Inside, the old brick oven had already been pulled out, and a builder's skip in the lane was filling up with rubble. When a reporter from the Hollowgum Herald finally reached Rosa by phone, she would only say, 'Good bread should be eaten, not thrown in a bin.' Then she hung up, because she was busy painting the new counter.
encounters.prompt: Why did Rosa give away all her bread on Thursday?
encounters.success: The bakery was closing for two weeks, and she says good bread shouldn't be thrown in a bin.

options.text: The bread had gone stale, and nobody would pay full price for it.
options.reason: The bread was still warm, and its smell drifted down the street.

options.text: She was retiring and wanted to say thank you.
options.reason: That fits the free bread, but the second sign says she'll be back in two weeks.

options.text: She wanted the Hollowgum Herald to write a story about her.
options.reason: She barely spoke to the reporter and then hung up.

options.text: She was closing for two weeks and didn't want the bread wasted.

encounters.frame: Someone summed up Beryl's letter to the Herald. One part is wrong.
encounters.text: Dear Editor, I am writing about my neighbour, Mr Desmond Pratt of 14 Wattle Street. His lawn is the neatest on the street, and he mows it every Saturday. At five o'clock last Saturday morning, while it was still dark, Mr Pratt started his lawnmower. It was so loud that it set off three dogs and a car alarm. He mowed his front lawn, his back lawn and, for some reason, the strip of grass outside the post office. I was furious, and I marched over in my dressing gown to complain. Mr Pratt was wearing a head torch and a very large straw hat. He simply pointed at the newspaper on his porch, where the headline read RECORD HEAT: 44 DEGREES BY MIDDAY. He told me that the last time he mowed at lunchtime in summer, he had to lie in the paddling pool for an hour afterwards. By nine o'clock he had finished and gone inside, and by noon the footpath was too hot to stand on in thongs. I still do not think anyone should mow in the dark. However, I would like to thank Mr Pratt for doing my lawn as well, which he did while I was getting dressed. Yours sincerely, Beryl Tonks

encounters.success: He pointed at the 44-degree headline and remembered nearly melting last time. He was beating the heat.

encounters.frame: Tully can't believe the coach took Jaz off. The Cubbler thinks there's a reason.
encounters.text: It was the last home game of the season. With six minutes left in the last quarter, the Reef Rays were leading the Sandflies by sixty-two points, and their star forward, Jaz Kemp, had already kicked eight goals. She had never kicked nine in a game, and the crowd was chanting her name. Her little brother was holding up a sign that said NINE! Then Coach Harris called for a change. Jaz jogged to the bench, looked up at the scoreboard and threw her hands in the air. 'Coach! One more goal!' she pleaded. 'I feel great! I could run all day!' Coach Harris just shook his head and handed her a water bottle. Earlier in the week, he had told the local paper that the grand final against Seabreeze, the only team to beat the Rays all season, was next Saturday. 'We'll need every player fit and firing for that one,' he had said. 'I'm not taking any silly risks between now and then.' The two players sitting next to Jaz on the bench were the team's next-best forwards, and he had taken them off ten minutes earlier. Jaz sulked for exactly three minutes, then cheered louder than anyone when a teammate kicked the final goal.
encounters.prompt: Why did Coach Harris take Jaz off?
encounters.success: The grand final is next week, he wants everyone fit, and the game was already won. He was protecting her.
